title: Where were you, Krishna?
hook: Draupadi tells her friend Krishna that even he failed her, and he hears every word
carry: sakhya: you can tell God everything

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where a vessel from the sun fed every guest, and Draupadi ate last. Your line was surya: the sun who ripens food for all.

Chariots on a forest road. Word has reached Krishna's people that the Pandavas are in exile, and Krishna comes to find them. The cousins embrace. Then Draupadi speaks, and she doesn't make small talk. She tells him everything: the hall, being dragged in by her hair, the laughter, the husbands who sat silent. She weeps as she speaks. And under all of it is one question she doesn't quite need to say out loud. Where were you?
screen: `KRISHNA COMES TO THE FOREST.` → `DRAUPADI TELLS EVERYTHING.` → `WHERE WERE YOU?`

segments.voice: Draupadi doesn't tidy her grief. She names each wrong, in order, to the one person she trusts to hear it whole. In the epic's telling, she gives him four reasons he should protect her: they're family, her dignity, his power to help, and one more word worth holding onto, sakhya, their friendship. Then the hardest thing: she has no husband, no son, no brother, not even Krishna, because none of them protected her. Krishna, whom devotees worship as God, doesn't scold her. He makes her a promise: the women of those who wronged her will one day weep as she is weeping now. Then, turning to Yudhishthira, he answers the question underneath. Had I been in Dvaraka, I would have come to that game uninvited and stopped it. But he was away, fighting a king named Shalva, who had attacked his city. Draupadi speaks to Krishna as a friend, and in Hindu devotion that's a real way to love God. It's called sakhya: friendship with God. In the Bhagavata Purana, the boy Prahlada lists nine ways of devotion, and friendship is one of them; devotees often name Draupadi and Arjuna as its great examples. A friend can say the hard thing. So many Hindus feel free to bring God everything: grief, anger, even 'where were you?' Many teachers read the scene that way: devotion isn't only polite praise. Honest words, said to God and heard all the way through, are prayer too.
screen: `DRAUPADI NAMES EACH WRONG.` · `NOT EVEN YOU, KRISHNA.` · `I WAS FIGHTING SHALVA.` · then, large: `SAKHYA: GOD AS A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: If you have a home shrine, sit before it; if not, anywhere quiet will do. Tell God, Krishna, or the holy as you know it, one true thing you've been holding back: a hurt, a disappointment, a 'where were you'. Say it plainly, in your own words, the way Draupadi spoke to her friend. Then stay a few breaths and let yourself be heard. If you don't pray, say it to the quiet, or write it down, and let it be heard all the way through.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi tells her friend Krishna everything, and he hears it all.
Your line: sakhya: you can tell God everything. Draupadi did, and Krishna heard her to the end. Tomorrow: is forgiving always right? Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.

howItsDone: Devotees revere Krishna as God, and storytellers dwell on this forest meeting, where Draupadi pours out her grief to her friend; sakhya, loving God as a friend, is counted among the classic ways of Hindu devotion.

Krishna.meaning: the Pandavas' cousin and friend, worshipped by devotees as God

Shalva.meaning: a king who attacked Dvaraka in a flying citadel

Draupadi.meaning: wife of the five Pandava brothers

sakhya.meaning: friendship; in devotion, loving God as a friend

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli that Draupadi lists husbands, sons, friends, brothers and Krishna as those who failed her, and that Krishna's promise concerns the weeping of the wives of her tormentors.
Confirm Krishna's statement that he would have come uninvited to the game had he been in Dvaraka, and that he was fighting Shalva of the Saubha (flying city).

Popular tellings place Krishna's help to Draupadi in the hall (the endless garment); the script avoids contradicting that and focuses on this forest conversation. A Keeper may want a line acknowledging the hall tradition.
